"Yamini, your school sent a form about the summer art camp. Why didn't you show me?"
Yamini kept stirring the dal. "It doesn't matter, Papa."
Vaibhav put the paper on the counter. "You love drawing."
"You would have said no."
"Would I?"
"You always said no. Tuition first, then we'll see. For three years." She shrugged. "So I stopped asking."
Vaibhav was quiet. "That was when I lost the job. Money was tight. It's different now."
"Okay."
"Yamini, I mean it. Do you want to go?"
She looked at the form for a long time, then back at the pot. "I don't know. I don't really think about wanting things anymore."
Vaibhav set a pen on top of the form. "Then think about it tonight. I'll ask again in the morning."

qa.q: What was the school form about?
qa.a: The summer art camp.

qa.q: What does Yamini mean by "I don't really think about wanting things anymore"?
qa.a: After three years of her wishes being turned down, she has stopped expecting a yes, so wanting feels pointless, even now that things have changed.

qa.q: What choice by Vaibhav could help break the pattern?
qa.a: Explaining why he said no before, and promising to ask again in the morning, gives Yamini time and a real chance to voice a want.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav feel when he hears "So I stopped asking"?
qa.a: He falls quiet, probably realising with sadness that the hard years taught his daughter not to ask, even after they ended.

grounding: A teenager whose wishes were turned down for years no longer asks for anything, even now that her father could say yes.

subtype: Not asking for help at home [Actor]
passage: For years, whenever I asked for something at home, a cycle, a phone of my own, a place on the school trip, the answer was "not now" or nothing at all, because my grandmother was ill and everyone was stretched thin. So I stopped asking. Last month my parents actually asked me what I wanted for my seventeenth birthday, and my mouth just opened and closed. I said, "Nothing, anything's fine." My friend Rehana couldn't believe it. "Jyoti, they're asking! Things are okay at your place now." I know that. My head knows that. But part of me still waits quietly, as if asking is a door that doesn't open. I'm trying to say one small want out loud each week. This week it was "Can we have dosa on Sunday?" We did.

qa.q: What did Jyoti ask for this week?
qa.a: "Can we have dosa on Sunday?"

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's mouth just open and close when asked about the birthday?
qa.a: Jyoti felt caught off guard and unsure; after years of "not now", Jyoti had stopped expecting wishes to matter, so even a genuine offer found nothing ready to say.

qa.q: What choice is Jyoti making to change the old belief?
qa.a: Saying one small want out loud each week, so each yes, like the Sunday dosa, becomes proof that asking can work now.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's parents feel hearing "Nothing, anything's fine"?
qa.a: They may feel puzzled or sad, having finally been able to ask, and not realise their child learned to stop asking during the hard years.

grounding: A teenager who learned that requests went unanswered still does not voice wishes after home life improves.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Maria, Class 10 check-ins, 3 October
Dilnaz came in about her falling science marks. When I asked if anyone at home could help, she said, "I don't ask them for things." She explained, flatly, that for years her requests went unanswered while her parents worked double shifts; now her mother has a daytime job and is home in the evenings, but Dilnaz still doesn't ask. She sat with her hands tucked under her legs and looked at the floor. She didn't seem upset, more resigned, as if asking had stopped being an option.
What I did: we practised one sentence she could say at home tonight: "Can you sit with me for my science for twenty minutes?" She agreed to try once and tell me on Friday. With her permission, I'll also phone her mother.

qa.q: What sentence did Maria and Dilnaz practise?
qa.a: "Can you sit with me for my science for twenty minutes?"

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's flat, resigned manner suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems to believe asking is useless, a belief left from years of unanswered requests, so she isn't upset, just not expecting anything.

qa.q: Which choice by Maria gives Dilnaz a realistic first step?
qa.a: Practising one short, specific request and asking her to try it once, so she can test whether home has changed.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's mother react to the phone call?
qa.a: She may be surprised and sad to learn Dilnaz doesn't feel able to ask, and glad to know how to help now that she is home in the evenings.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager who stopped asking for help at home after years of being unanswered, though things have changed.

passage:
Tuesday
Yogesh Chacha asked at dinner what I want for my birthday. Everyone looked at me. I said, "Anything is fine." He said, "No, really, Swati. What would make you happy?" I said it again. Anything.
The truth is I want a sketchbook, the thick one with cream pages. But in the old house nobody ever heard what I wanted. Five cousins, one room, everybody tired. I stopped asking around Class 6. It just seemed smarter.
Chachi said, "You can tell us later if you think of something." She said it so gently.
Here it's different. Nobody laughs. They ask twice. I know that. So why does my mouth still say "anything"?
Maybe tomorrow I'll write "sketchbook" on a chit and leave it on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Swati actually want for the birthday?
qa.a: A sketchbook, the thick one with cream pages.

qa.q: Why does Swati still say 'anything' even though things have changed?
qa.a: Swati still feels wary of asking: years of wishes going unheard in the old house taught Swati that asking was pointless, and that belief speaks first even with people who ask twice.

qa.q: What small step does Swati consider, and why might it be a good start?
qa.a: Writing 'sketchbook' on a chit for the fridge; it is a low-risk way to voice a wish and find out that here it is heard.

qa.q: How might Yogesh Chacha feel hearing 'Anything is fine' twice?
qa.a: He may feel a little sad and puzzled, wanting to make Swati happy, and aware it will take patience for Swati to trust that wishes matter now.

grounding: A teenager whose wishes went unheard in a crowded home no longer voices them, even in a new home that listens.
